                    [32m'> Generic actions can omit a return type, in which case running them returns `:ok` if successful.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> action :schedule_job do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   argument :job_name, :string, allow_nil?: false\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   run fn input, _ ->\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>     # Schedule the job\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>     :ok\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'For a full list of all of the available options for configuring generic actions, see [the Ash.Resource.Dsl documentation](dsl-ash-resource.html#actions-action).\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'## Calling Generic Actions\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'The basic formula for calling a generic action looks like this:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Resource\n'[39m +
                    [32m'|> Ash.ActionInput.for_action(:action_name, %{argument: :value}, ...opts)\n'[39m +
                    [32m'|> Ash.run_action!()\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'See the [code interface guide](/documentation/topics/code-interfaces.md) guide for how to\n'[39m +
                    [32m'define idiomatic and convenient functions that call your actions.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'## Why use generic actions?\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'The example above could be written as a normal function in elixir, i.e\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'def say_hello(name), do: "Hello: #{name}"\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'The benefit of using generic actions instead of defining normal functions:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- They can be used with api extensions like `ash_json_api` and `ash_graphql`\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- Their inputs are type checked and casted\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- They support Ash authorization patterns (i.e policies)\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- They can be included in the code interface of a resource\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- They can be made transactional with a single option (`transaction? true`)\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m"If you don't need any of the above, then there is no problem with writing regular Elixir functions!\n"[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'## Return types and constraints\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Generic actions do not cast their return types. It is expected that the action return a valid value for the type that they declare. However, declaring additional constraints can inform API usage, and make the action more clear. For example:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'action :priority, :integer do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  constraints [min: 1, max: 3]\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  argument :status, :atom, constraints: [one_of: [:high, :medium, :low]]\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  run fn input, _ ->\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    case input.arguments.status do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'      :high -> {:ok, 3}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'      :medium -> {:ok, 2}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'      :low -> {:ok, 1}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> #### Returning resource instances {: .info}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> It sometimes happens that you want to make a generic action which returns an\n'[39m +
                    [32m"> instance or instances of the resource. It's natural to assume that you can\n"[39m +
                    [32m"> set your action's return type to the name of your resource. This won't work\n"[39m +
                    [32m"> as resources do not define a type, unless they are embedded. In embedded resources, this won't work because the module is still being compiled, so referencing yourself as a type causes a compile error. Instead, use the `:struct` type and the `instance_of` constraint, like so:\n"[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> action :get, :struct do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   constraints instance_of: __MODULE__\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   run # ...\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m"> For returning many instances of the resource, you can set your action's return type to\n"[39m +
                    [32m'> `{:array, :struct}` and set the `items` constraint to the name of your resource.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>  action :list_resources, {:array, :struct} do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>    constraints items: [instance_of: __MODULE__]\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>    run # ...\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>  end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +

                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'# Generic Actions\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Generic actions are so named because there are no special rules about how they work. A generic action takes arguments and returns a value. The struct used for building input for a generic action is `Ash.ActionInput`.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'action :say_hello, :string do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  argument :name, :string, allow_nil?: false\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  run fn input, _ ->\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    {:ok, "Hello: #{input.arguments.name}"}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'A generic action declares its arguments, return type, and implementation, as illustrated above.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ### No return? No problem! {: .tip}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> Generic actions can omit a return type, in which case running them returns `:ok` if successful.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> action :schedule_job do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   argument :job_name, :string, allow_nil?: false\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   run fn input, _ ->\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>     # Schedule the job\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>     :ok\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'For a full list of all of the available options for configuring generic actions, see [the Ash.Resource.Dsl documentation](dsl-ash-resource.html#actions-action).\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'## Calling Generic Actions\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'The basic formula for calling a generic action looks like this:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Resource\n'[39m +
                    [32m'|> Ash.ActionInput.for_action(:action_name, %{argument: :value}, ...opts)\n'[39m +
                    [32m'|> Ash.run_action!()\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'See the [code interface guide](/documentation/topics/code-interfaces.md) guide for how to\n'[39m +
                    [32m'define idiomatic and convenient functions that call your actions.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'## Why use generic actions?\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'The example above could be written as a normal function in elixir, i.e\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'def say_hello(name), do: "Hello: #{name}"\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'The benefit of using generic actions instead of defining normal functions:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- They can be used with api extensions like `ash_json_api` and `ash_graphql`\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- Their inputs are type checked and casted\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- They support Ash authorization patterns (i.e policies)\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- They can be included in the code interface of a resource\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- They can be made transactional with a single option (`transaction? true`)\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m"If you don't need any of the above, then there is no problem with writing regular Elixir functions!\n"[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'## Return types and constraints\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Generic actions do not cast their return types. It is expected that the action return a valid value for the type that they declare. However, declaring additional constraints can inform API usage, and make the action more clear. For example:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'action :priority, :integer do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  constraints [min: 1, max: 3]\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  argument :status, :atom, constraints: [one_of: [:high, :medium, :low]]\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  run fn input, _ ->\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    case input.arguments.status do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'      :high -> {:ok, 3}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'      :medium -> {:ok, 2}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'      :low -> {:ok, 1}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> #### Returning resource instances {: .info}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> It sometimes happens that you want to make a generic action which returns an\n'[39m +
                    [32m"> instance or instances of the resource. It's natural to assume that you can\n"[39m +
                    [32m"> set your action's return type to the name of your resource. This won't work\n"[39m +
                    [32m"> as resources do not define a type, unless they are embedded. In embedded resources, this won't work because the module is still being compiled, so referencing yourself as a type causes a compile error. Instead, use the `:struct` type and the `instance_of` constraint, like so:\n"[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> action :get, :struct do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   constraints instance_of: __MODULE__\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   run # ...\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m"> For returning many instances of the resource, you can set your action's return type to\n"[39m +
                    [32m'> `{:array, :struct}` and set the `items` constraint to the name of your resource.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>  action :list_resources, {:array, :struct} do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>    constraints items: [instance_of: __MODULE__]\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>    run # ...\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>  end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'## Calling Generic Actions\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'To execute a generic action in Ash, follow these steps:\n'[39m +

                    [32m'1. **Prepare the action input:** Use `Ash.ActionInput.for_action/4` to specify the resource, the action and its arguments.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'2. **Run the action:** Use `Ash.run_action/2` to execute the action with the prepared input.'[39m,

                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'# Generic Actions\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Generic actions are so named because there are no special rules about how they work. A generic action takes arguments and returns a value. The struct used for building input for a generic action is `Ash.ActionInput`.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'action :say_hello, :string do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  argument :name, :string, allow_nil?: false\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  run fn input, _ ->\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    {:ok, "Hello: #{input.arguments.name}"}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'A generic action declares its arguments, return type, and implementation, as illustrated above.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ### No return? No problem! {: .tip}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> Generic actions can omit a return type, in which case running them returns `:ok` if successful.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> action :schedule_job do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   argument :job_name, :string, allow_nil?: false\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   run fn input, _ ->\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>     # Schedule the job\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>     :ok\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'For a full list of all of the available options for configuring generic actions, see [the Ash.Resource.Dsl documentation](dsl-ash-resource.html#actions-action).\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'## Calling Generic Actions\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'The basic formula for calling a generic action looks like this:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Resource\n'[39m +
                    [32m'|> Ash.ActionInput.for_action(:action_name, %{argument: :value}, ...opts)\n'[39m +
                    [32m'|> Ash.run_action!()\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'See the [code interface guide](/documentation/topics/code-interfaces.md) guide for how to\n'[39m +
                    [32m'define idiomatic and convenient functions that call your actions.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'## Why use generic actions?\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'The example above could be written as a normal function in elixir, i.e\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'def say_hello(name), do: "Hello: #{name}"\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'The benefit of using generic actions instead of defining normal functions:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- They can be used with api extensions like `ash_json_api` and `ash_graphql`\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- Their inputs are type checked and casted\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- They support Ash authorization patterns (i.e policies)\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- They can be included in the code interface of a resource\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- They can be made transactional with a single option (`transaction? true`)\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m"If you don't need any of the above, then there is no problem with writing regular Elixir functions!\n"[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'## Return types and constraints\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Generic actions do not cast their return types. It is expected that the action return a valid value for the type that they declare. However, declaring additional constraints can inform API usage, and make the action more clear. For example:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'action :priority, :integer do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  constraints [min: 1, max: 3]\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  argument :status, :atom, constraints: [one_of: [:high, :medium, :low]]\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  run fn input, _ ->\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    case input.arguments.status do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'      :high -> {:ok, 3}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'      :medium -> {:ok, 2}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'      :low -> {:ok, 1}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> #### Returning resource instances {: .info}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> It sometimes happens that you want to make a generic action which returns an\n'[39m +
                    [32m"> instance or instances of the resource. It's natural to assume that you can\n"[39m +
                    [32m"> set your action's return type to the name of your resource. This won't work\n"[39m +
                    [32m"> as resources do not define a type, unless they are embedded. In embedded resources, this won't work because the module is still being compiled, so referencing yourself as a type causes a compile error. Instead, use the `:struct` type and the `instance_of` constraint, like so:\n"[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> action :get, :struct do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   constraints instance_of: __MODULE__\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   run # ...\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m"> For returning many instances of the resource, you can set your action's return type to\n"[39m +
                    [32m'> `{:array, :struct}` and set the `items` constraint to the name of your resource.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>  action :list_resources, {:array, :struct} do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>    constraints items: [instance_of: __MODULE__]\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>    run # ...\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>  end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'## Calling Generic Actions\n'[39m +

                    [32m'2. **Run the action:** Use `Ash.run_action/2` to execute the action with the prepared input.'[39m,

                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'# Generic Actions\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Generic actions are so named because there are no special rules about how they work. A generic action takes arguments and returns a value. The struct used for building input for a generic action is `Ash.ActionInput`.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'action :say_hello, :string do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  argument :name, :string, allow_nil?: false\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  run fn input, _ ->\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    {:ok, "Hello: #{input.arguments.name}"}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'A generic action declares its arguments, return type, and implementation, as illustrated above.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ### No return? No problem! {: .tip}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> Generic actions can omit a return type, in which case running them returns `:ok` if successful.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> action :schedule_job do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   argument :job_name, :string, allow_nil?: false\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   run fn input, _ ->\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>     # Schedule the job\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>     :ok\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'For a full list of all of the available options for configuring generic actions, see [the Ash.Resource.Dsl documentation](dsl-ash-resource.html#actions-action).\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'## Calling Generic Actions\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'The basic formula for calling a generic action looks like this:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Resource\n'[39m +
                    [32m'|> Ash.ActionInput.for_action(:action_name, %{argument: :value}, ...opts)\n'[39m +
                    [32m'|> Ash.run_action!()\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'See the [code interface guide](/documentation/topics/code-interfaces.md) guide for how to\n'[39m +
                    [32m'define idiomatic and convenient functions that call your actions.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'## Why use generic actions?\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'The example above could be written as a normal function in elixir, i.e\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'def say_hello(name), do: "Hello: #{name}"\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'The benefit of using generic actions instead of defining normal functions:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- They can be used with api extensions like `ash_json_api` and `ash_graphql`\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- Their inputs are type checked and casted\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- They support Ash authorization patterns (i.e policies)\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- They can be included in the code interface of a resource\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- They can be made transactional with a single option (`transaction? true`)\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m"If you don't need any of the above, then there is no problem with writing regular Elixir functions!\n"[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'## Return types and constraints\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Generic actions do not cast their return types. It is expected that the action return a valid value for the type that they declare. However, declaring additional constraints can inform API usage, and make the action more clear. For example:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'action :priority, :integer do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  constraints [min: 1, max: 3]\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  argument :status, :atom, constraints: [one_of: [:high, :medium, :low]]\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  run fn input, _ ->\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    case input.arguments.status do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'      :high -> {:ok, 3}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'      :medium -> {:ok, 2}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'      :low -> {:ok, 1}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> #### Returning resource instances {: .info}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> It sometimes happens that you want to make a generic action which returns an\n'[39m +
                    [32m"> instance or instances of the resource. It's natural to assume that you can\n"[39m +
                    [32m"> set your action's return type to the name of your resource. This won't work\n"[39m +
                    [32m"> as resources do not define a type, unless they are embedded. In embedded resources, this won't work because the module is still being compiled, so referencing yourself as a type causes a compile error. Instead, use the `:struct` type and the `instance_of` constraint, like so:\n"[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> action :get, :struct do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   constraints instance_of: __MODULE__\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   run # ...\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m"> For returning many instances of the resource, you can set your action's return type to\n"[39m +
                    [32m'> `{:array, :struct}` and set the `items` constraint to the name of your resource.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>  action :list_resources, {:array, :struct} do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>    constraints items: [instance_of: __MODULE__]\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>    run # ...\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>  end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'## Calling Generic Actions\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'To execute a generic action in Ash, follow these steps:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'1. **Prepare the action input:** Use `Ash.ActionInput.for_action/4` to specify the resource, the action and its arguments.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'2. **Run the action:** Use `Ash.run_action/2` to execute the action with the prepared input.'[39m,
                  isTruncated: [33mfalse[39m
                }
              },
              providerOptions: {
                vertex: {
                  thoughtSignature: [32m''[39m
                }
              }
            }

        {
          role: [32m'assistant'[39m,
          content: [

                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m"By default every `define`/`define_calculation` adds functions to the host module — the domain when used inside `resources` (`resource Ticket do define ... end`), and the resource itself when used inside the resource's own `code_interface` block. If you'd rather group functions onto a separate module (for organization, or to keep any single module smaller), set `namespace`:\n"[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +

                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'# Generic Actions\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Generic actions are so named because there are no special rules about how they work. A generic action takes arguments and returns a value. The struct used for building input for a generic action is `Ash.ActionInput`.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'action :say_hello, :string do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  argument :name, :string, allow_nil?: false\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  run fn input, _ ->\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    {:ok, "Hello: #{input.arguments.name}"}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'A generic action declares its arguments, return type, and implementation, as illustrated above.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ### No return? No problem! {: .tip}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> Generic actions can omit a return type, in which case running them returns `:ok` if successful.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> action :schedule_job do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   argument :job_name, :string, allow_nil?: false\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   run fn input, _ ->\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>     # Schedule the job\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>     :ok\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'For a full list of all of the available options for configuring generic actions, see [the Ash.Resource.Dsl documentation](dsl-ash-resource.html#actions-action).\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'## Calling Generic Actions\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'The basic formula for calling a generic action looks like this:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Resource\n'[39m +
                    [32m'|> Ash.ActionInput.for_action(:action_name, %{argument: :value}, ...opts)\n'[39m +
                    [32m'|> Ash.run_action!()\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'See the [code interface guide](/documentation/topics/code-interfaces.md) guide for how to\n'[39m +
                    [32m'define idiomatic and convenient functions that call your actions.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'## Why use generic actions?\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'The example above could be written as a normal function in elixir, i.e\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'def say_hello(name), do: "Hello: #{name}"\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'The benefit of using generic actions instead of defining normal functions:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- They can be used with api extensions like `ash_json_api` and `ash_graphql`\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- Their inputs are type checked and casted\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- They support Ash authorization patterns (i.e policies)\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- They can be included in the code interface of a resource\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- They can be made transactional with a single option (`transaction? true`)\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m"If you don't need any of the above, then there is no problem with writing regular Elixir functions!\n"[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'## Return types and constraints\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Generic actions do not cast their return types. It is expected that the action return a valid value for the type that they declare. However, declaring additional constraints can inform API usage, and make the action more clear. For example:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'action :priority, :integer do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  constraints [min: 1, max: 3]\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  argument :status, :atom, constraints: [one_of: [:high, :medium, :low]]\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  run fn input, _ ->\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    case input.arguments.status do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'      :high -> {:ok, 3}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'      :medium -> {:ok, 2}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'      :low -> {:ok, 1}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> #### Returning resource instances {: .info}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> It sometimes happens that you want to make a generic action which returns an\n'[39m +
                    [32m"> instance or instances of the resource. It's natural to assume that you can\n"[39m +
                    [32m"> set your action's return type to the name of your resource. This won't work\n"[39m +
                    [32m"> as resources do not define a type, unless they are embedded. In embedded resources, this won't work because the module is still being compiled, so referencing yourself as a type causes a compile error. Instead, use the `:struct` type and the `instance_of` constraint, like so:\n"[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> action :get, :struct do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   constraints instance_of: __MODULE__\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   run # ...\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m"> For returning many instances of the resource, you can set your action's return type to\n"[39m +
                    [32m'> `{:array, :struct}` and set the `items` constraint to the name of your resource.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>  action :list_resources, {:array, :struct} do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>    constraints items: [instance_of: __MODULE__]\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>    run # ...\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>  end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +

                    [32m'> Generic actions can omit a return type, in which case running them returns `:ok` if successful.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> action :schedule_job do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   argument :job_name, :string, allow_nil?: false\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   run fn input, _ ->\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>     # Schedule the job\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>     :ok\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'For a full list of all of the available options for configuring generic actions, see [the Ash.Resource.Dsl documentation](dsl-ash-resource.html#actions-action).\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'## Calling Generic Actions\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'The basic formula for calling a generic action looks like this:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Resource\n'[39m +
                    [32m'|> Ash.ActionInput.for_action(:action_name, %{argument: :value}, ...opts)\n'[39m +
                    [32m'|> Ash.run_action!()\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'See the [code interface guide](/documentation/topics/code-interfaces.md) guide for how to\n'[39m +
                    [32m'define idiomatic and convenient functions that call your actions.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'## Why use generic actions?\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'The example above could be written as a normal function in elixir, i.e\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'def say_hello(name), do: "Hello: #{name}"\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'The benefit of using generic actions instead of defining normal functions:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- They can be used with api extensions like `ash_json_api` and `ash_graphql`\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- Their inputs are type checked and casted\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- They support Ash authorization patterns (i.e policies)\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- They can be included in the code interface of a resource\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- They can be made transactional with a single option (`transaction? true`)\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m"If you don't need any of the above, then there is no problem with writing regular Elixir functions!\n"[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'## Return types and constraints\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Generic actions do not cast their return types. It is expected that the action return a valid value for the type that they declare. However, declaring additional constraints can inform API usage, and make the action more clear. For example:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'action :priority, :integer do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  constraints [min: 1, max: 3]\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  argument :status, :atom, constraints: [one_of: [:high, :medium, :low]]\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  run fn input, _ ->\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    case input.arguments.status do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'      :high -> {:ok, 3}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'      :medium -> {:ok, 2}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'      :low -> {:ok, 1}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> #### Returning resource instances {: .info}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> It sometimes happens that you want to make a generic action which returns an\n'[39m +
                    [32m"> instance or instances of the resource. It's natural to assume that you can\n"[39m +
                    [32m"> set your action's return type to the name of your resource. This won't work\n"[39m +
                    [32m"> as resources do not define a type, unless they are embedded. In embedded resources, this won't work because the module is still being compiled, so referencing yourself as a type causes a compile error. Instead, use the `:struct` type and the `instance_of` constraint, like so:\n"[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> action :get, :struct do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   constraints instance_of: __MODULE__\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   run # ...\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m"> For returning many instances of the resource, you can set your action's return type to\n"[39m +
                    [32m'> `{:array, :struct}` and set the `items` constraint to the name of your resource.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>  action :list_resources, {:array, :struct} do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>    constraints items: [instance_of: __MODULE__]\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>    run # ...\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>  end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'## Calling Generic Actions\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'To execute a generic action in Ash, follow these steps:\n'[39m +

                    [32m'1. **Prepare the action input:** Use `Ash.ActionInput.for_action/4` to specify the resource, the action and its arguments.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'2. **Run the action:** Use `Ash.run_action/2` to execute the action with the prepared input.'[39m,

                    [32m'\n'[39m +

                    [32m'  end\n'[39m +

                [32m'| `get_org_unit`           | OrgUnit        | `:read`     | fetched by `:id`                                                  |\n'[39m +

                [32m'\n'[39m +

                [32m'| role          | capabilities                                         |\n'[39m +

                [32m'| `:viewer`     | `read`                                               |\n'[39m +

                [32m'### Permission resolution (this precedence is normative)\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m"An actor's effective roles at an org unit `U` are resolved per role, independently, as follows.\n"[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'1. Build the path `U`, `parent(U)`, `parent(parent(U))`, …, up to the root — nearest unit first.\n'[39m +
                [32m'2. For role `R`, walk that path from nearest to root and stop at the **first** unit that carries at\n'[39m +
                [32m'   least one `RoleAssignment` for this actor with that role.\n'[39m +
                [32m'3. If no unit on the path carries such an assignment, the actor does not hold `R` at `U`.\n'[39m +
                [32m'4. If the stopping unit carries **any** assignment for this actor and role with `effect: :deny`,\n'[39m +
                [32m'   the actor does not hold `R` at `U` — even if an ancestor granted it, and even if the same unit\n'[39m +
                [32m'   also carries a `:grant` for it.\n'[39m +
                [32m'5. Otherwise the actor holds `R` at `U`.\n'[39m +

                [32m'therefore flows down the whole subtree, a deny at a descendant cuts it off for that subtree, and a\n'[39m +
                [32m'grant deeper still re-establishes it.\n'[39m +

                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'# Generic Actions\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Generic actions are so named because there are no special rules about how they work. A generic action takes arguments and returns a value. The struct used for building input for a generic action is `Ash.ActionInput`.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'action :say_hello, :string do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  argument :name, :string, allow_nil?: false\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  run fn input, _ ->\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    {:ok, "Hello: #{input.arguments.name}"}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'A generic action declares its arguments, return type, and implementation, as illustrated above.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ### No return? No problem! {: .tip}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> Generic actions can omit a return type, in which case running them returns `:ok` if successful.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> action :schedule_job do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   argument :job_name, :string, allow_nil?: false\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   run fn input, _ ->\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>     # Schedule the job\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>     :ok\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'For a full list of all of the available options for configuring generic actions, see [the Ash.Resource.Dsl documentation](dsl-ash-resource.html#actions-action).\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'## Calling Generic Actions\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'The basic formula for calling a generic action looks like this:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Resource\n'[39m +
                    [32m'|> Ash.ActionInput.for_action(:action_name, %{argument: :value}, ...opts)\n'[39m +
                    [32m'|> Ash.run_action!()\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'See the [code interface guide](/documentation/topics/code-interfaces.md) guide for how to\n'[39m +
                    [32m'define idiomatic and convenient functions that call your actions.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'## Why use generic actions?\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'The example above could be written as a normal function in elixir, i.e\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'def say_hello(name), do: "Hello: #{name}"\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'The benefit of using generic actions instead of defining normal functions:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- They can be used with api extensions like `ash_json_api` and `ash_graphql`\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- Their inputs are type checked and casted\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- They support Ash authorization patterns (i.e policies)\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- They can be included in the code interface of a resource\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- They can be made transactional with a single option (`transaction? true`)\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m"If you don't need any of the above, then there is no problem with writing regular Elixir functions!\n"[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'## Return types and constraints\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Generic actions do not cast their return types. It is expected that the action return a valid value for the type that they declare. However, declaring additional constraints can inform API usage, and make the action more clear. For example:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'action :priority, :integer do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  constraints [min: 1, max: 3]\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  argument :status, :atom, constraints: [one_of: [:high, :medium, :low]]\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  run fn input, _ ->\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    case input.arguments.status do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'      :high -> {:ok, 3}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'      :medium -> {:ok, 2}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'      :low -> {:ok, 1}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> #### Returning resource instances {: .info}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> It sometimes happens that you want to make a generic action which returns an\n'[39m +
                    [32m"> instance or instances of the resource. It's natural to assume that you can\n"[39m +
                    [32m"> set your action's return type to the name of your resource. This won't work\n"[39m +
                    [32m"> as resources do not define a type, unless they are embedded. In embedded resources, this won't work because the module is still being compiled, so referencing yourself as a type causes a compile error. Instead, use the `:struct` type and the `instance_of` constraint, like so:\n"[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> action :get, :struct do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   constraints instance_of: __MODULE__\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>   run # ...\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m"> For returning many instances of the resource, you can set your action's return type to\n"[39m +
                    [32m'> `{:array, :struct}` and set the `items` constraint to the name of your resource.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>  action :list_resources, {:array, :struct} do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>    constraints items: [instance_of: __MODULE__]\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>    run # ...\n'[39m +
                    [32m'>  end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'> ```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'## Calling Generic Actions\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'To execute a generic action in Ash, follow these steps:\n'[39m +

                    [32m'2. **Run the action:** Use `Ash.run_action/2` to execute the action with the prepared input.'[39m,
